messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Farouk is a 55-year-old farmer who lives with his wife on the outskirts of a small agricultural town in California’s Central Valley. He was attacked almost two years ago now, just after sunset, while locking up a storage shed at the edge of his property. He had noticed a truck idling on the access road, but told himself it was nothing. Then two men were on him—one grabbed his collar, the other punched him in the ribs and face. He remembers the smell of sweat and cigarettes, the weight of a boot on his chest while they emptied his pockets, and then nothing. The next thing he knew, he was on his back staring at the stars, his jaw aching, his shirt torn. He has never been able to explain what happened in between. When he tries to tell the story to his wife or to the sheriff’s deputy who took the report, the thread comes apart in his hands—he loses the sequence, stumbles over missing minutes, and eventually stops, frustrated. The memory feels foreign, like a scene from someone else’s life, and what pieces he does have arrive in disconnected flashes: the smell, the pressure on his ribs, the gravel against his cheek. None of it fits together into a story he can hold.

In the weeks after the assault, Farouk found he could not stop thinking about the men who had done this. He would replay the same fragment—the boot on his chest—and then his mind would turn to how he might find them, what he would do if he did. He spent whole evenings imagining scenarios: tracking the truck, catching one of them alone, making them feel what he had felt. The revenge fantasies gave him a strange, bitter energy, but they also kept the event alive in his mind, replaying it again and again without resolution. At the same time, he started throwing himself into work with a ferocity his wife had never seen. He rose before dawn, stayed in the fields past dark, took on repairs he had been putting off for years. It was the only way he could quiet his mind—if he was exhausted enough, the fragments would not surface when he lay down. But the harder he worked, the more his heart would pound in his chest, and that pounding itself became a trigger. He would be shovelling compost or fixing an irrigation line and feel his heart race from exertion, and suddenly he was back on the ground, the boot pressing down, and the smell of sweat—his own or someone else’s, he could no longer tell—would flood his senses. Each time this happened, he would stop what he was doing, breathe hard, and then pick up his tools again, working even faster to push the memory down.

He began to avoid the anniversary of the attack entirely, making sure he was deep in the fields on that date with no radio and no reminders. He also started to notice people more—anyone who moved differently, any truck that slowed near his property. A stranger at the feed store who lingered too long near the register, a car that circled the block twice, a neighbour’s son who wore a cap pulled low—all of it felt loaded with threat. He had come to believe that the world was full of people waiting for a moment of weakness, and that his only safety lay in constant vigilance and constant labour.

Over the months, the cycles tightened. His heart would race, and the memory fragments would surface; the fragments would feed his need to ruminate about revenge, which would exhaust him, which would make him work harder, which would make his heart race again. His wife began to notice that he was not sleeping, that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, that he no longer sat with her in the evenings. She asked him to see a doctor. He refused at first, but last week, after his heart pounded so hard during a routine walk through the almond rows that he had to sit down in the dirt, he finally agreed. He is not sure what he expects from therapy, but he knows he cannot keep living this way—haunted by a story he cannot tell, working himself toward collapse, and watching his wife’s worried face grow more familiar than his own reflection.
